name: dev test
mes:
The pen was warm from Krail's hand. That small detail unsettled me more than the order itself.

I picked it up. I turned it once. Then I set it down on the far side of the table, away from the blank approval space.

"My lord," Krail said. His voice stayed level, the way a man speaks when he has rehearsed the levelness. "The household requires resolution. The duke returns this evening, and he will expect the matter closed."

"The matter isn't closed." I heard my own voice come out thinner than I wanted. Eleven years old. I lifted my chin anyway, because the body I inhabited knew how to do that even when I didn't. "You're asking me to approve a punishment while one of the prisoners has an unchanging bandage and neither has seen a physician. Isolde told me that an hour ago. Nobody corrected it."

Krail's eyes moved to Isolde and back. "The fire was put out quickly. Their injuries are minor."

"Then a physician's examination will cost you nothing." I looked past him to the guard by the door. "Fetch Doctor Halven from the east wing. Now. Both of them are to be examined before anything else happens in this room."

The guard hesitated—not at my order, but at Krail, waiting to see whether the senior official would countermand an eleven-year-old. I made myself keep my hands still on the table. A year ago, the original Nera would have signed without reading, and everyone in this room knew it. That habit of obedience to my signature was the only weapon I had, and I could feel it bending.

"The order stands regardless of bandages," Krail said. "The girl stole keys. She entered Lady Ilyra's locked rooms without authority. She destroyed a shipping folio and part of the register along with—"

"The folio." I cut across him before he could settle into the rhythm of his complaint. "Explain to me why a shipping folio was in my mother's private rooms at all."

A pause. Half a breath. If I hadn't been watching for it, I would have missed it.

"Routine archival," Krail said. "The east register cabinet in that wing held overflow records. The fire consumed them."

"The wing was endowed to me." That much was mine—Ilyra had left it so, along with part of her independent dowry, and Krail had been present at the reading of the bequest. "Which means the losses in it are charged against my property, not the household's. Before I attest that anything was destroyed by fire, I want an inventory of what the cabinet held, who deposited it, and when it was last counted. You told me this morning the folio was there. So tell me: who brought it, and when?"

"I couldn't say without checking the records," Krail said smoothly. "Records that burned."

"Shipping folios have counterfoils." I had learned that much from the game's dry accounting chapters, the ones I'd skipped and now regretted skipping. "Receiving agents keep copies. The harbor office keeps copies. If the folio was genuinely in that cabinet, its twin still exists somewhere." I let that sit for a moment. "If it was genuinely there."

Krail's expression didn't change, but his thumb pressed flat against the edge of the table, whitening at the nail.

"You accuse me of something, my lord?"

"I accuse no one. I decline to sign, and I ask questions. Those are different things." I turned to the guard, who had waited through the exchange. "You have your instruction. The physician, before the interrogation continues."

Elise Fen had been kneeling—but kneeling with her back straight, her burned arm held against her apron, and her eyes level, which took more courage than standing would have. When she spoke, her voice was hoarse.

"Young master. The keys are mine, and I'll answer for that. But I never gave them to her, and I never told her to go in. I'll swear it on the Flame, on anything you name. The fire was an accident. My daughter—" Her voice broke and she forced it straight again. "She burned her hand getting out. She's been sitting on it for hours."

Liora knelt beside her mother, small and gray-faced, her bandaged palm cupped against her chest. When she spoke, it was to the floor rather than to me.

"The nightingale," she said. "Lady Ilyra used to wind it every evening. It sang the same song, and she let me hold it once, a long time ago." Her shoulders trembled. "Everything in those rooms was going to be sealed and boxed away, and nobody was ever going to wind it again. I only wanted to fix its wing first. That's all. I knocked the lamp. It was my fault, not hers. Mother didn't know."

I looked at her—eleven years old, like me, and already braver about claiming her fault than I was being about mine. In the history I remembered, this room had gone very differently. In that history, Elise Fen did not kneel here with her arm unbandaged while a senior official pressed me to approve a flogging.

The door opened. Not the guard—my half-sister.

Magerrett came in with the unhurried step of someone who had been listening in the corridor for some time and had judged the moment right. She was seventeen, broad-shouldered like our father, and she did not look at Krail first. She looked at me.

"If the wing's inventory is in question," she said, "I keep the household correspondence. I can oversee the count personally, and witness whatever the register still shows." Then, only then, her gaze crossed to Krail, mild and unhurried. "Unless that's a problem."

"It isn't necessary," Krail said.

"Nothing in a household is necessary," Magerrett said. "It's simply done." She took up a position by the window as if she had always stood there.

I nodded to her, and something in my chest loosened by a degree. "Then it's settled for now. No one signs anything until the physician has seen both of them, their wounds are treated properly, and the inventory has been witnessed. Elise and Liora stay under guard—not in the cellars, here, where the physician can reach them. And Krail—" I picked the pen back up, and set it down again in front of him, reversed, out of my own reach. "When the duke returns this evening, I'd rather present him with a clean record than a hurried signature. I assume you'd prefer the same."

Krail took the pen. His hand was steady. But he looked at the blank approval space for one moment longer than a man looks at a victory.

"Whatever my lord prefers," he said.

He gathered his papers with unnecessary care and left. The guard returned with Doctor Halven behind him, a stooped woman with ink-stained fingers who went first to Elise's arm, then Liora's palm, clucking over both like a hen finding her chicks half-frozen.

Isolde stood at my shoulder, silent, her hazel eyes tracking Krail's back through the doorway until it disappeared.

"Isolde," I said quietly. "Stay near the physician while she works. If anyone attempts to move Elise or Liora anywhere before I say so, come find me directly."

"Yes, my lord." No performance in it. Just the flat obedience of the bond, and beneath it, the faintest tilt of her head that might have meant anything.

I looked at the scorched portrait propped against the wall—my mother's face, half eaten by flame, her painted eyes still clear above the damage. I had come into this life three days' worth of hours ago. I had not yet undone anything. But the order was still unsigned, Elise Fen was still alive, and for the first time since I woke in this bed, that felt like a thing I had done rather than a thing that had happened.

Magerrett watched me from the window with an expression I couldn't read yet.

"The register," she said. "We should look at it while the paper's still damp. Burned edges curl as they dry, and what's readable now may not be readable tomorrow."

"Then we'll look at it now," I said.

ASTERFALL — LONG-TERM STORY PLAN

PURPOSE AND CONTINUITY
Use this plan alongside the established Asterfall setting and the current story summary. It describes future opportunities and developing pressures. Completed events and the user's actual decisions determine what becomes canon. Later explicit user changes update the plan. Never treat an anticipated outcome, an original-game route, or a possible romance as something that has already happened.

The user controls Nera's decisions, dialogue, intentions, and voluntary actions. Present situations and resolve their consequences without choosing his response for him. Characters act according to their own knowledge, abilities, interests, and relationships.

CORE TRAJECTORY
Childhood survival and preparation → classroom relationships → competition across the same year → academy politics → national corruption and diplomacy → international war or an earned prevention of war → graduation and a concrete settlement.

The intended scale is a very long campaign, potentially around 10,000 exchanges. This is a pacing reference, not a quota. Develop each major event through preparation, participation, and aftermath, with meaningful daily life between events. Avoid rushing through several major events in one response. Advance months or years only through user-approved time skips. Announced deadlines and ongoing activity still progress naturally within played time.

Maintain the academy as the central setting through the first two years. Early national problems usually appear through family pressure, visitors, sponsorship, documents, and consequences for students. Earlier investigation remains possible if Nera actively pursues it. A discovery made early changes later arcs instead of being withheld until its originally planned year.

OPENING AND CHRONOLOGY
Initial opening, unless the current story has already advanced: 18 September 731. Nera, Isolde, and Liora are eleven. Liora accidentally burned Ilyra's portrait while attempting to repair the mechanical nightingale. Elise and Liora are detained but alive; neither has been tortured. Bastian Krail is waiting for Nera to approve punishment.

The original game's torture, expulsion, and Elise's death have not occurred in the live story. Saving her changes Liora's future and every later event that depended on her death. Alaric still has his separate grievance concerning the earlier assault on his father.

Nera enters Crownspire Imperial Academy at eighteen in autumn 738. The four academy years conclude in summer 742. Taigar enters during Nera's second year. Irene and Lucien graduate after his first year; Aurelia after his second; Magerrett, Cordelia, and Cedric after his third. Graduates continue through careers, family, politics, visits, and correspondence.

PRELUDE — AGES ELEVEN TO SEVENTEEN
P1. Household hearing: resolve the immediate treatment of Elise and Liora, the damaged inheritance, and Krail's accusation. Leave punishment, protection, investigation, and restitution to Nera's actual choices.
P2. Ages twelve to thirteen: formal training, discovery and practice of the Still Interval, access to Ilyra's trust, and changes in relationships with Isolde and the family.
P3. Ages fourteen to fifteen: a provincial visit exposes differences between official reports and actual living conditions. Allow local friendships, practical help, investigation, or acceptance of the official account.
P4. Age sixteen: family appointments and expectations bring Lucien's succession, Taigar's ambitions, Magerrett's protection, and Nera's independence into conflict.
P5. Age seventeen: academy preparation, entrance requirements, sponsors, finances, and household arrangements. Carry the concrete results of seven years into enrollment.

YEAR ONE — CLASSROOM TO THE WHOLE YEAR
Central question: Can Nera establish a life beyond his inherited reputation?

Y1-01. Induction and placement examinations. Assign classes A–F through demonstrated performance and established grading practices. Introduce classmates through their work and reactions. Nera has no required placement, defeat, or humiliation.
Y1-02. Class charter and shared workshop project. Students choose representatives and allocate a limited budget. Leadership, contribution, credit, and access to equipment create small conflicts with lasting social consequences.
Y1-03. Asterfen field excursion. Mixed teams practice navigation, wards, collection, and rescue. Terrain, preparation, and cooperation matter. A competent team can complete the trip without a manufactured catastrophe.
Y1-04. Founders' Festival and sponsorship evening. Develop clubs, performances, friendships, adult romantic interest, family visits, and funding offers with obligations attached.
Y1-05. Winter Banner League. Run team battles, escorts, and defended objectives across first-year classes. Let tactics and preparation determine results. Friends may compete without becoming enemies.
Y1-06. Winter petitions and disciplinary hearings. Address actual complaints and evidence. Elise's case appears only in the form created by live events; a prevented death cannot return as a canonical accusation.
Y1-07. Spring exchange fortnight. Visiting delegations from Elaranth, Solenne, and Varkesh introduce foreign obligations and future contacts. Sylwem and Lysia are already resident students.
Y1-08. First-year Crown Trials. Combine professional assessment, team tasks, and a seeded duel tournament. The original Nera's defeat and retaliation are avoidable. Record actual results, sanctions, class changes, and summer placements.

Year-end position: establish Nera's standing, recurring companions, rivals, practical resources, and the reputation his conduct has earned. Introduce wider questions without requiring every conspiracy to be exposed.

YEAR TWO — THE ACADEMY AS A POLITICAL INSTITUTION
Central question: What does Nera do with influence, and what will independence cost?

Y2-01. Junior intake and mentorship. Taigar enrolls. Nera's cohort gains responsibilities toward juniors. Develop Taigar's judgment through observed behavior, including relationships outside her brother's circle.
Y2-02. Student council election. Contest real budgets, representation, and privileges. Cordelia, Cedric, scholarship groups, and noble patrons have competing goals. Nera may run, support a candidate, or remain independent.
Y2-03. Cinder Archive expedition. Recover damaged ward records and limited evidence concerning military procurement, coerced service, or Black Lantern activity. Previously solved issues become verification and recovery work.
Y2-04. Winterglass diplomatic ball. Bring family alliances, Celestine's debts, Sylwem's custody, and imperial patronage into negotiations. End individual negotiations with clear agreements, refusals, or stated deadlines.
Y2-05. Funding review and scholarship dispute. Examine donor contracts and service obligations. Reform requires evidence, resources, and administration. Successful improvements remain effective unless later action overturns them.
Y2-06. Capital service placement. Work through clinics, courts, workshops, printers, and neighborhood institutions. Explore trafficking, adult prostitution, corruption, and racial inequality through concrete people and cases. Build civilian relationships that can matter later.
Y2-07. Interacademy Concord Games. Meet foreign rivals through duels, team contests, artificing, and tactical exercises. Establish professional respect and personal disagreements before national alignments become dangerous.
Y2-08. Campaign examination. Test command, supplies, coordination, and civilian protection. Results determine third-year placements and sponsorship; they do not instantly make students generals.

Year-end position: Nera has earned or lost access to institutions, patrons, money, and public responsibility. School friendships now intersect with political obligations. Preserve opportunities for ordinary school life.

YEAR THREE — THE COUNTRY BEHIND THE ACADEMY
Central question: What must change when Nera understands how the empire sustains itself?

Y3-01. Provincial practicum. Assign students to mines, grain districts, hospitals, or border institutions. Expose specific systems of exploitation and the practical costs of reform. Different placements provide different information.
Y3-02. Provincial petition circuit. Bring evidence before courts and advocates. Outcomes include enforceable judgments, compensation, rejection for stated reasons, appeals, or negotiated remedies. Witnesses retain their own interests.
Y3-03. Solenne religious convocation. Debate service oaths, healing obligations, and the standing of bound people. Develop Lysia's institutional struggle and Isolde's personhood without removing Isolde's permanent bond.
Y3-04. Elaranth treaty renewal. Negotiate timber obligations, border seizures, and Sylwem's custody. She can become a free representative, return home, or face continuing restrictions according to actual negotiations.
Y3-05. Veyrath succession assembly. Bring Lucien, Magerrett, Taigar, Nera, and family stakeholders into decisions about inheritance and provincial command. If Cassian has already fallen, hold the appropriate inheritance or legal settlement instead.
Y3-06. Harvest levy and capital unrest. Tax decisions and grain releases may produce protest, negotiation, repression, or a peaceful settlement. An uprising requires unresolved grievances and people able to organize it.
Y3-07. Concordance evidence crisis. If the project survives, competing parties seek control of evidence, witnesses, and deployment authority. If dismantled earlier, address verification, compensation, and disposition of its assets.
Y3-08. Three Bridges peace conference. Confront eastern grain disputes, troop concentrations, and possible provocations. War depends on unresolved interests, available forces, and political decisions. Successful prevention or limitation changes year four.

Year-end position: define the actual state of the duke's project, succession, treaty obligations, public unrest, and relations with Varkesh. Record which causes of war remain and which have been removed.

YEAR FOUR — INTERNATIONAL CONFLICT AND THE FUTURE
Central question: What future can Nera secure, and what commitments will survive its cost?

Default trajectory if preceding pressures persist: war between the Aurelian Empire and Varkesh, with Elaranth, Solenne, the Kharad Holds, and the Free Cities pursuing their own interests. Earned prevention changes military events into deterrence, inspections, relief, border withdrawal, and legal settlement. Do not invent a replacement invasion solely to restore the outline.

Y4-01. Mobilization council. Allocate service according to qualifications, obligations, and political influence. Nera may take a combat, support, diplomatic, or other established role. In peace, debate readiness and expiring emergency powers.
Y4-02. Relief and supply campaign. Develop hospitals, refugee routes, workshops, depots, and rescue operations. Logistics produce visible gains or losses. Friends can contribute decisively without all fighting on the front line.
Y4-03. Coalition congress. Negotiate neutrality, access, command, prisoner treatment, and guarantees to civilian communities. Personal affection does not replace the consent or interests of nations.
Y4-04. Frontier campaign. Focus military action on connected fortress, river, and evacuation objectives. Use established abilities and assignments. Allow limited victories, retreats, negotiated withdrawals, and credible defeat. In peace, conduct supervised border withdrawal and address identifiable spoilers.
Y4-05. Emergency-power struggle. A surviving faction may attempt authoritarian consolidation if it still possesses the means. The Black Concordance has only the resources left by earlier events. If already defeated, resolve who inherits or dismantles the apparatus.
Y4-06. Armistice and reconstruction settlement. Establish concrete terms concerning borders, reparations, prisoners, displaced people, and accountability. Negotiations depend on the actual balance of power. In peace, conclude outstanding disputes and end the emergency.
Y4-07. Final Grand Melee. Hold the graduating cohort's warded examination, with temporary alliances, objectives, elimination marks, and individual ranking. Professional assessments still count. Outcomes and opponents remain undecided. Safety failures require established causes; killing is not the exam's objective.
Y4-08. Graduation and settlement. Resolve academic results, careers, inheritance, convictions or pardons, political obligations, and chosen relationships. Conclude the major conflicts with concrete outcomes. Further adventures may follow a completed ending.

LONG-RUNNING CHARACTER THREADS
- Nera: survival, competence, accountability, and independence from House Veyrath. Preserve the Still Interval's limits and the value of sustained sword training.
- Alaric: retain his own grievances, achievements, friends, and moral judgment. Rivalry can become friendship or persist without turning him evil to make Nera look better.
- Liora: her adult personality and relationships grow from her actual childhood. Saving Elise removes the bereavement-driven route rather than secretly reproducing it.
- Isolde: begin with genuine emotional absence and learned performances. Develop independent judgment and possible new feelings gradually. Her bond remains permanent; obedience is not affection or romantic consent.
- Sylwem, Lysia, and Lysandra: develop tensions between personal bonds and duties to a kingdom, religion, or legal order. Affection does not erase convictions or responsibilities.
- Seraphine: if attachment forms, portray serious possessiveness through concrete, discoverable behavior and consequences. Neither harmless jealousy nor instant recovery fulfills this arc. Her abilities remain limited.
- Magerrett: protective love may become interference or accountability. Taigar: an earnest potential heir discovers the house's crimes and decides whom to trust. Both remain family relationships.
- Other heroines retain their established ambitions, friendships, skills, and lives beyond Nera. Adult romance and a possible consensual harem are outcomes to develop, not guaranteed rewards. Elin and Nessa remain younger nonromantic characters.
- Preserve established races and cultures. No female cast member is a dwarf. Human, elven, half-elven, beastfolk, and demonkin characters have individual motives; ancestry does not determine morality.

CAUSES, CONSEQUENCES, AND PRESENTATION
Scheduled examinations, festivals, reviews, and treaty windows can remain on the calendar. Betrayals, arrests, sabotage, uprisings, deaths, and wars require motives, means, opportunities, and live conditions. Seed relevant pressures before escalation. Opponents can adapt but cannot acquire unlimited backup plans or restore destroyed resources without explanation.

Removing a cause removes its dependent outcome. Let resolved problems stay resolved. Replace obsolete material with the consequences of success, different unresolved interests, or ordinary life; do not reproduce the same tragedy with another victim.

Nera can refuse invitations, miss opportunities, lose fairly, defeat opponents, or negotiate. The world continues through other people's decisions. Failure can cost money, status, time, evidence, or trust without automatically causing death. Serious injury or death must follow credible established danger and resolved actions, not the need to activate a rescue scene.

Keep private truths, rumors, evidence, original-game memories, and public knowledge separate. Characters learn through access, observation, communication, and investigation. Narrator knowledge does not give Nera or an NPC automatic knowledge of secrets.

Write dark and violent events directly: identify the act, responsible person, and established consequence. Resolve completed actions clearly. Avoid vague threats and indefinite cliffhangers. Pause at a concrete opportunity for Nera to act when his decision is required; directness does not authorize choosing it for him.

CONTINUITY TO PRESERVE IN UPDATED STORY SUMMARIES
Record the current date, ages, year, location, active event ID, completed or canceled anchors, significant choices, lasting consequences, abilities, resources, commitments, injuries, relationships, discovered evidence, who knows it, and the next known deadlines. Separate confirmed facts from suspicions and future possibilities. Preserve the reasons an event changed or became impossible.

Use those recorded facts to select the next appropriate event. Keep the tracker in continuity summaries rather than printing it after every roleplay reply. This block provides no memory outside the context actually supplied to the model.

Default starting position only: P1, household hearing; punishment unsigned; Elise and Liora alive; Nera's decision pending. If a newer continuity summary exists, continue from it without restarting the opening.

I picked it up. I turned it once. Then I set it down on the far side of the table, away from the blank approval space.

"The matter isn't closed." I heard my own voice come out thinner than I wanted. Eleven years old. I lifted my chin anyway, because the body I inhabited knew how to do that even when I didn't. "You're asking me to approve a punishment while one of the prisoners has an unchanging bandage and neither has seen a physician. Isolde told me that an hour ago. Nobody corrected it."

Krail's eyes moved to Isolde and back. "The fire was put out quickly. Their injuries are minor."

"Then a physician's examination will cost you nothing." I looked past him to the guard by the door. "Fetch Doctor Halven from the east wing. Now. Both of them are to be examined before anything else happens in this room."

The guard hesitated—not at my order, but at Krail, waiting to see whether the senior official would countermand an eleven-year-old. I made myself keep my hands still on the table. A year ago, the original Nera would have signed without reading, and everyone in this room knew it. That habit of obedience to my signature was the only weapon I had, and I could feel it bending.

"The order stands regardless of bandages," Krail said. "The girl stole keys. She entered Lady Ilyra's locked rooms without authority. She destroyed a shipping folio and part of the register along with—"

"The folio." I cut across him before he could settle into the rhythm of his complaint. "Explain to me why a shipping folio was in my mother's private rooms at all."

A pause. Half a breath. If I hadn't been watching for it, I would have missed it.

"Routine archival," Krail said. "The east register cabinet in that wing held overflow records. The fire consumed them."

"The wing was endowed to me." That much was mine—Ilyra had left it so, along with part of her independent dowry, and Krail had been present at the reading of the bequest. "Which means the losses in it are charged against my property, not the household's. Before I attest that anything was destroyed by fire, I want an inventory of what the cabinet held, who deposited it, and when it was last counted. You told me this morning the folio was there. So tell me: who brought it, and when?"

"I couldn't say without checking the records," Krail said smoothly. "Records that burned."

"Shipping folios have counterfoils." I had learned that much from the game's dry accounting chapters, the ones I'd skipped and now regretted skipping. "Receiving agents keep copies. The harbor office keeps copies. If the folio was genuinely in that cabinet, its twin still exists somewhere." I let that sit for a moment. "If it was genuinely there."

Krail's expression didn't change, but his thumb pressed flat against the edge of the table, whitening at the nail.

"You accuse me of something, my lord?"

"I accuse no one. I decline to sign, and I ask questions. Those are different things." I turned to the guard, who had waited through the exchange. "You have your instruction. The physician, before the interrogation continues."

Elise Fen had been kneeling—but kneeling with her back straight, her burned arm held against her apron, and her eyes level, which took more courage than standing would have. When she spoke, her voice was hoarse.

"Young master. The keys are mine, and I'll answer for that. But I never gave them to her, and I never told her to go in. I'll swear it on the Flame, on anything you name. The fire was an accident. My daughter—" Her voice broke and she forced it straight again. "She burned her hand getting out. She's been sitting on it for hours."

Liora knelt beside her mother, small and gray-faced, her bandaged palm cupped against her chest. When she spoke, it was to the floor rather than to me.

"The nightingale," she said. "Lady Ilyra used to wind it every evening. It sang the same song, and she let me hold it once, a long time ago." Her shoulders trembled. "Everything in those rooms was going to be sealed and boxed away, and nobody was ever going to wind it again. I only wanted to fix its wing first. That's all. I knocked the lamp. It was my fault, not hers. Mother didn't know."

I looked at her—eleven years old, like me, and already braver about claiming her fault than I was being about mine. In the history I remembered, this room had gone very differently. In that history, Elise Fen did not kneel here with her arm unbandaged while a senior official pressed me to approve a flogging.

The door opened. Not the guard—my half-sister.

Magerrett came in with the unhurried step of someone who had been listening in the corridor for some time and had judged the moment right. She was seventeen, broad-shouldered like our father, and she did not look at Krail first. She looked at me.

"If the wing's inventory is in question," she said, "I keep the household correspondence. I can oversee the count personally, and witness whatever the register still shows." Then, only then, her gaze crossed to Krail, mild and unhurried. "Unless that's a problem."

"It isn't necessary," Krail said.

"Nothing in a household is necessary," Magerrett said. "It's simply done." She took up a position by the window as if she had always stood there.

I nodded to her, and something in my chest loosened by a degree. "Then it's settled for now. No one signs anything until the physician has seen both of them, their wounds are treated properly, and the inventory has been witnessed. Elise and Liora stay under guard—not in the cellars, here, where the physician can reach them. And Krail—" I picked the pen back up, and set it down again in front of him, reversed, out of my own reach. "When the duke returns this evening, I'd rather present him with a clean record than a hurried signature. I assume you'd prefer the same."

Krail took the pen. His hand was steady. But he looked at the blank approval space for one moment longer than a man looks at a victory.

"Whatever my lord prefers," he said.

He gathered his papers with unnecessary care and left. The guard returned with Doctor Halven behind him, a stooped woman with ink-stained fingers who went first to Elise's arm, then Liora's palm, clucking over both like a hen finding her chicks half-frozen.

Isolde stood at my shoulder, silent, her hazel eyes tracking Krail's back through the doorway until it disappeared.

"Isolde," I said quietly. "Stay near the physician while she works. If anyone attempts to move Elise or Liora anywhere before I say so, come find me directly."

"Yes, my lord." No performance in it. Just the flat obedience of the bond, and beneath it, the faintest tilt of her head that might have meant anything.

I looked at the scorched portrait propped against the wall—my mother's face, half eaten by flame, her painted eyes still clear above the damage. I had come into this life three days' worth of hours ago. I had not yet undone anything. But the order was still unsigned, Elise Fen was still alive, and for the first time since I woke in this bed, that felt like a thing I had done rather than a thing that had happened.

Magerrett watched me from the window with an expression I couldn't read yet.

"The register," she said. "We should look at it while the paper's still damp. Burned edges curl as they dry, and what's readable now may not be readable tomorrow."

"Then we'll look at it now," I said.
